lessons.title: Emergency calling is a design gate
lessons.why: A phone system that cannot reach emergency services is not ready, even if every other demo looks good.
body: Treat emergency calling as a gate before go-live. Calling Plans in supported countries use Microsoft’s emergency service, and you still load locations. Direct Routing makes you, the SBC, and the carrier responsible for the call.

Do not test by placing a real emergency call. Use the carrier’s test process. Do not send emergency calls into a bot so they can be ‘handled.’ Know whether your recorder includes them, and follow the rule you were given.

chart.title: Gate, not a follow-up
chart.note: Do this before the pilot becomes production.

lessons.say: Emergency is a gate. I will not demo a bot on the emergency number.
lessons.listen: Finish emergency location and a local route before go-live. Test with the carrier’s process, not a real emergency call.

lessons.title: Dynamic location
lessons.why: A laptop moves. The address you shouted at install time does not.
body: Dynamic emergency calling uses the network Teams can see. In the usual design that means trusted IPs, sites, and subnets tied to validated civic addresses. A dispatchable location is specific enough for responders. One address for five buildings is not.

Trusted IPs mean ‘this client is inside our network.’ If you list the VPN concentrator, every remote user looks internal. Give the VPN pool no dispatchable headquarters address. The same subnet list should later feed location-based routing and CQD, or the three maps will disagree.
lessons.say: Trusted IP, subnet, civic address. The VPN pool is not headquarters.
lessons.fault: Remote users inherit the HQ floor because the VPN range was trusted as internal.
lessons.listen: Map trusted IPs, subnets, and civic addresses. Do not give VPN users the headquarters address.

lessons.title: Calling Plans versus Direct Routing emergency
lessons.why: The client is Teams in both designs. The carrier is not.
body: On Calling Plans, Microsoft’s emergency calling path is in play in supported countries, and your job is accurate locations. On Direct Routing, the emergency voice route must prefer the local SBC, and the carrier must accept the call. PIDF-LO can ride in the INVITE. If the SBC strips it, the far end may only see the trunk.
An emergency calling policy controls notification and lookup. It is not a substitute for the route. On-site security who are not notified will meet responders at the wrong door.
lessons.say: Calling Plan emergency and Direct Routing emergency are different owners. I will not copy one route onto the other.
lessons.fault: A Calling Plan user’s 911 is forced out a foreign SBC.
lessons.listen: Say who routes the emergency call. Microsoft’s path for Calling Plans, your SBC and carrier for Direct Routing.

lessons.title: Location-based routing
lessons.why: Some countries treat toll bypass as a regulatory problem. Location-based routing is the Teams control.
depends: gateways that belong to those sites
body: Location-based routing stops a user in a regulated site from placing or receiving PSTN through a gateway in another site. It uses the same kind of network topology as emergency location. A traveler’s laptop should not egress through another country’s SBC.
Media bypass can fight this if the media path would egress in the wrong place. Read the current LBR article before you enable bypass at a regulated site. Do not invent an exception in a workshop.
lessons.say: LBR keeps PSTN in-country. I will re-read it before I enable media bypass there.
lessons.fault: A laptop in one country places PSTN through another country’s SBC.
lessons.listen: Location-based routing stops toll bypass by tying users to local gateways. Check it before you enable media bypass.

lessons.title: Survivable Branch Appliance
lessons.why: A WAN cut should not remove the ability to place a local PSTN call, including emergency.
body: A Survivable Branch Appliance keeps a limited calling set for clients that can reach it when Microsoft 365 cannot. It is a Direct Routing feature. Meetings, presence, and the rest of the cloud are not the survivable set. Confirm the feature list for the firmware you run.
Test a WAN cut in a window. An SBA that has never been tested is a packing slip. Analog devices such as elevators need a path that does not depend on a Teams user signed in through the dead WAN.

chart.title: During a WAN cut
chart.note: Teaching split. Confirm the appliance feature list.

lessons.say: SBA is local PSTN survivability for Direct Routing, not a full Teams cloud.
lessons.fault: The WAN fails and emergency calls fail with it because no local path was tested.
lessons.listen: A Survivable Branch Appliance keeps local PSTN up when the branch cannot reach Microsoft 365. Test the cut.

lessons.title: Notification and the test call
lessons.why: Responders at the wrong door, and a test that called the real emergency service, are both failures.
body: Assign the emergency calling policy that notifies the people who can meet responders. Test the notification. A policy that exists and is not assigned notifies nobody.
Use the carrier’s test number or process. Do not dial the real emergency number from a lab because you were curious. Record the result: location shown, SBC used, who was notified.
lessons.say: I test emergency with the carrier’s process and I check that on-site notification fired.
lessons.fault: The notification policy exists and is assigned to nobody.
lessons.listen: Assign the notification policy and test emergency calling with the carrier’s process, not a real emergency call.
